saved_turn.question: how do they show that the ultraviolet glow of the sky tracks how much dust dims starlight?
saved_turn.answer:
They test this in the low-dust North Galactic Pole region, comparing GALEX maps of diffuse ultraviolet light with Planck’s \(E(B-V)\) reddening map—a measure of how much dust reddens and dims starlight. Both maps were put on the same 6-arcminute grid, and the analysis was restricted to Galactic latitudes \(b>70^\circ\). [1] [2]

The evidence is a positive, roughly linear relation between ultraviolet brightness and reddening. But it is noisy pixel by pixel: the raw FUV correlation was only \(\rho=0.536\), which the authors attribute to other UV emission and photon-counting noise. They estimated pixel uncertainties, rejected outliers, then averaged surviving pixels in narrow reddening bins. The binned FUV relation was much tighter, \(\rho=0.993\), with fitted relation \(\mathrm{FUV}=2285.3\,E(B-V)+278.6\). In other words, after accounting for scatter, brighter diffuse FUV generally marks more reddening. [3] [4]

They also check the inferred dust map against other measures: it correlates strongly with neutral hydrogen column density, and its quasar-based extinction estimates agree closely with Planck’s; comparison with a Pan-STARRS stellar reddening map also favors the GALEX-based values in this region. [5]

So the claim is supported by a map-to-map trend plus independent checks—not by UV brightness alone. The direct pixel-level relationship is considerably weaker than the binned one, and the study’s result is for the North Galactic Pole, not yet a demonstration that the same relation holds across the whole sky. [3] [6]

citations.quote: 2 DATA 2.1 Dust Emission The GALEX (Galaxy Evolution Explorer) mission (Martin et al. 2005; Morrissey et al. 2007) surveyed a substantial portion of the sky in two ultraviolet bands: the far-ultraviolet (FUV; 1528 ˚A) and the near-ultraviolet (NUV; 2360 ˚A). Murthy (2014) used these observations to generate sky maps of the diffuse cosmic radiation at 2 ′ spatial resolution by masking the point sources, subtracting the foreground, and removing the airglow contribution from both bands and the zodiacal light from the NUV band. Higher-resolution (15 ′′ ) versions of these maps are available via Zenodo 1 . From these we constructed a diffuse-emission map of the NGP region (𝑏 > 70 ◦ ) at 6 ′ pixel resolution, matching the resolution of the Planck observations (described below). Fig. 1 shows the resulting two-dimensional FUV and NUV intensity maps from GALEX (left and middle) in photon units, photons cm -2 s -1 sr -1 ˚A -1 . The map is centred on the North Galactic Pole (𝑙 = 0 ◦ , 𝑏 = 90 ◦ ), with concentric circles marking every 10 ◦ in latitude and sectors divided into 45 ◦ segments, progressing clockwise with longitude (0 ◦ < 𝑙 < 360 ◦ ). Darker regions indicate areas with no GALEX coverage. Both datasets reveal prominent filamentary structures in the lower-right portions of the images. These filaments were first identified in the polarization studies of Hilditch et al. (1976) and Markkanen (1979), and originate from dust clouds at ∼ 100-300 pc (Gontcharov & Mosenkov 2019). We took the E(B-V) maps from the Planck mission (Planck Collaboration et al. 2014, 2016a). Planck Collaboration et al. (2016a) fitted these all-sky observations with the silicate-graphite-PAH dust model of Draine & Li (2007) to map the reddening over the entire sky. Planck combined the WISE and IRAS data to produce a full allsky dust-emission map of the Milky Way at 6 ′ resolution, which we resampled to match the GALEX maps (Fig. 1, right). At the NGP the reddening is low (E(B - V) ≈ 0.02-0.05 mag), whereas the perpixel Planck uncertainty is ∼ 5 mmag. The uncertainty is therefore a large fraction of the reddening signal itself, so individual Planck pixels carry substantial fractional errors in the derived E(B-V) (Wolf 2014; Casandjian et al. 2022). This motivates the binning and outlierrejection approach adopted in Section 3.

1 INTRODUCTION Interstellar extinction refers to the attenuation of starlight caused by absorption and scattering as it passes through the interstellar medium and must be corrected for in order to derive the intrinsic spectrum of any source in the sky. Accurate determination of extinction depends on the availability of nearby stars of known spectral type whose extinction can be measured as a function of wavelength (Fitzpatrick 1999; Fitzpatrick & Massa 2007) and large-scale surveys used proxies such as 21 cm radiation (Burstein & Heiles 1978) and, more recently, the infrared emission from thermally emitting dust grains (Schlegel et al. 1998). The current maps are those from Planck data (Planck Collaboration et al. 2014) at a spatial resolution of ∼ 5 ′ - 6 ′ . However, the infrared emission is dependent on the composition and size distribution of the grains and the temperature of each component and the conversion from observed surface brightness to reddening may be variable over the sky (Casandjian et al. 2022). Boissier et al. (2015) proposed that a better tracer of extinction at higher spatial resolution would be the far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX). The dust is optically thin at high Galactic latitudes, and dust-scattered far-UV (FUV) light should serve as a better tracer of extinction at higher spatial resolution than possible from available infrared observations. ★ E-mail: shalima.p@manipal.edu We have used GALEX observations to derive an extinction map around the North Galactic Pole (NGP), where the extinction is low (E(B-V) < 0.1 mag). The diffuse FUV here is dominated by dustscattered starlight (the diffuse Galactic light), which is directly proportional to the reddening. Other Galactic emission from the interstellar medium-molecular-hydrogen fluorescence, two-photon continuum, and line emission, also scales with the gas column, while a large constant offset arises from the extragalactic background light and airglow (Akshaya et al. 2019; Murthy 2014). We describe the data collection and processing in Section 2 and present the data analysis in Section 3. In Section 3 we also derive the extinction of quasars from our GALEX FUV and Planck maps and examine their relation with redshift (z), and we test the reddening derived from the GALEX FUV in the following sections. We compare our results with the optical stellar observations of Schlafly et al. (2014) and the quasar extinction maps with both the GALEX and Planck maps, and finally conclude on the use of FUV emission as a tracer of extinction relative to Planck or Schlegel.

We used the uncertainty maps of both GALEX bands, together with the Planck uncertainty map (taken directly from Planck Collaboration et al. 2016), to reject outliers as shown in Fig. 3. We characterised the GALEX intensity-reddening relation in three ways. First, the all-pixel correlation: using every pixel that passed the latitude cut (𝑏 > 70 ◦ ), with no outlier rejection, we found only a moderate pixelto-pixel correlation (FUV: 𝜌 = 0.536; NUV: 𝜌 = 0.243), owing to the large per-pixel scatter from 𝐻2 fluorescence, line emission and photon-counting noise (Fig. 2). This motivates the rejection and binning steps. Second, the Least Squares method: after rejecting outliers, we performed a weighted least-squares fit to the surviving individual pixels (Fig. 3), obtaining zero-reddening intercepts (offsets) of 278.6 (FUV) and 547.2 (NUV) photons cm -2 s -1 sr -1 ˚A -1 . Third, the Binning after rejection (centroid) method: we grouped the surviving pixels into equal 0.003 mag bins of E(B-V) , took the mean GALEX intensity in each bin, and fitted these binned centroids. The parameters for all cases are listed in Table 1. The three methods yield mutually consistent results. The correlation coefficient increases from the allpixel value (0.536 for FUV, 0.243 for NUV) to the least-squares fit after outlier rejection (0.662, 0.490) and is highest for the binned centroids (0.993, 0.976). This progression is attributed to the successive suppression of random scatter rather than to any change in the underlying relation: the outlier rejection removes the non-dust ultraviolet excess, and the binning averages out the residual per-pixel noise, so that the correlation improves at fixed slope. The binned centroids lie almost exactly along the least-squares fit, except the NUV above 0.04 mag, where the apparent falloff is of purely statistical origin, arising from the small number of surviving pixels at high E(B-V) after rejection. The agreement between the centroid and per-pixel least-squares intercepts (279.8 and 278.6, respectively) confirms that the relation between GALEX intensity and reddening is robust despite the substantial per-pixel scatter. We use the least-squares fit after the outlier rejection as given below.

ABSTRACT Interstellar extinction at high Galactic latitude is often traced by thermal dust emission, but the conversion from infrared surface brightness to reddening is sensitive to grain properties and temperature. We test dust-scattered far-ultraviolet (FUV) and near-ultraviolet (NUV) diffuse emission as a high-resolution extinction tracer towards the North Galactic Pole (NGP), where 𝐸 (𝐵-𝑉) < 0.1 mag. Using the GALEX diffuse maps of Murthy (2014), we build FUV and NUV intensity maps at 6 ′ resolution over the region 𝑏 > 70 ◦ and compare them with the Planck 𝐸 (𝐵-𝑉) map at matched resolution. A direct pixel-to-pixel regression gives only moderate correlations (𝜌 = 0.536 for FUV, 0.243 for NUV) owing to high per-pixel scatter from H2 fluorescence, line emission, and photon-counting noise; we therefore construct per-pixel GALEX uncertainty maps and apply a centroid-fitting method that fits the mean intensity in bins of 𝐸 (𝐵-𝑉) after rejection of outliers in an iterative sigma-clipping method, recovering tight relations (𝜌 = 0.993 for FUV, 0.976 for NUV). We find the best-fit relations for the FUV and NUV intensity per 6 ′ ×6 ′ pixel: FUV = 2285.3 𝐸 (𝐵-𝑉) + 278.6 and NUV = 1517.6 𝐸 (𝐵-𝑉) + 547.2 (photons cm -2 s -1 sr -1 ˚A -1 ) that are inverted to produce a 601 × 601 GALEX reddening map. GALEX E(B-V) correlates strongly with the 𝐻𝐼 column density from the all-sky HI4PI survey(𝜌 = 0.991). We validate the maps using SDSS quasars as extragalactic extinction calibrators: quasar extinctions from the GALEX and Planck maps agree with a correlation of 0.99 and a slope of 0.986. Comparison with the Pan-STARRS1 stellar reddening map of Schlafly et al. (2014) shows that the GALEX -based values have a smaller mean difference (0.039 mag) than with the Planck-based values (0.064 mag). These results establish dust-scattered FUV diffuse emission as a viable alternative to thermal-dust extinction maps at high Galactic latitude. Key words: ISM: dust, extinction - ISM: atoms - methods: statistical

7 CONCLUSION We have constructed a far-ultraviolet (FUV) extinction map of the North Galactic Pole region (𝑏 > 70 ◦ ), where the reddening is low (E(B-V) < 0.1 mag), and assessed dust-scattered FUV diffuse emission as a tracer of Galactic extinction. A direct pixel-to-pixel regression yielded only moderate correlations (𝜌 = 0.536 for FUV and 𝜌 = 0.243 for NUV). This scatter reflects the additional per-pixel contributions frommolecular-hydrogen fluorescence, interstellar line emission, and photon-counting noise rather than a weakness of the underlying relation. To recover the intrinsic relation, we constructed per-pixel GALEX uncertainty maps. We applied a centroid-fitting method to estimate the mean intensity in E(B-V) bins after iteratively sigma-clipping outliers. This increased the correlations to 𝜌 = 0.993 (FUV) and 𝜌 = 0.976 (NUV) and gave the best-fit relations FUV = 2285.3 E(B - V) +278.6 and NUV = 1517.6 E(B - V) +547.2 (photon units). The fitted offsets are consistent with the non-reddeningcorrelated background (extragalactic background light and airglow) reported in previous works (Akshaya et al. 2018, 2019). Inverting these relations, we produced a 601 × 601 GALEX-based reddening map of the NGP. We validated the maps in three independent ways. First, both the GALEX and Planck maps correlate strongly with the H I column density from the HI4PI survey (HI4PI Collaboration et al. 2016) (𝜌 = 0.991 and 0.988, respectively), confirming that the FUV diffuse emission traces the gas and dust column. Second, using SDSS quasars as extragalactic extinction calibrators, the quasar extinctions derived from the GALEX and Planck maps agree closely (correlation 0.99, slope 0.986). Third, a comparison with the Pan-STARRS1 stellar reddening map of Schlafly et al. (2014) shows that the GALEX-based reddening has a smaller mean difference (0.039 mag, 𝜎 = 0.019) than the Planck-based reddening (0.064 mag, 𝜎 = 0.034), indicating that the FUV-derived map is at least as accurate as the thermal-dust map at high Galactic latitude. Figure 12. QSO extinction measured using GALEX in comparison with stellar observations of Pan-STARRS1 by Schlafly et al. (2014)(right). Side by side is plotted with Planck (left) and Schlafly et al. The mean fit of the extinction values of the quasars is shown by the blue line.

7.1 Future work A potential advantage of far-ultraviolet diffuse emission as an extinction tracer is its finer native pixel scale compared to Planck's data. Planck achieves a maximum resolution of approximately 6 ′ , whereas GALEX (Morrissey et al. 2007; Murthy 2025) provides farultraviolet diffuse emission maps at a resolution of 15 ′′ . As part of future efforts, we plan to extend the analysis to regions below 𝑏 = 70 ◦ , testing whether the FUV-Planck relation derived here for the North Galactic Pole holds at other, lower Galactic latitudes. This would allow dereddening corrections to be validated over a larger sky area, and facilitate analysis of dust properties using an independent tracer relative to Planck. The GALEX and Planck reddening maps of the North Galactic Pole produced in this work are publicly available at https://github.com/swagatastro98/NGP_resources.

The current maps are those from Planck data (Planck Collaboration et al. 2014) at a spatial resolution of ∼ 5 ′ - 6 ′ . However, the infrared emission is dependent on the composition and size distribution of the grains and the temperature of each component and the conversion from observed surface brightness to reddening may be variable over the sky (Casandjian et al. 2022). Boissier et al. (2015) proposed that a better tracer of extinction at higher spatial resolution would be the far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX). The diffuse FUV here is dominated by dustscattered starlight (the diffuse Galactic light), which is directly proportional to the reddening. Other Galactic emission from the interstellar medium-molecular-hydrogen fluorescence, two-photon continuum, and line emission, also scales with the gas column, while a large constant offset arises from the extragalactic background light and airglow (Akshaya et al. 2019; Murthy 2014). We describe the data collection and processing in Section 2 and present the data analysis in Section 3. In Section 3 we also derive the extinction of quasars from our GALEX FUV and Planck maps and examine their relation with redshift (z), and we test the reddening derived from the GALEX FUV in the following sections. We compare our results with the optical stellar observations of Schlafly et al. (2014) and the quasar extinction maps with both the GALEX and Planck maps, and finally conclude on the use of FUV emission as a tracer of extinction relative to Planck or Schlegel.

We used the uncertainty maps of both GALEX bands, together with the Planck uncertainty map (taken directly from Planck Collaboration et al. 2016), to reject outliers as shown in Fig. 3. We characterised the GALEX intensity-reddening relation in three ways. First, the all-pixel correlation: using every pixel that passed the latitude cut (𝑏 > 70 ◦ ), with no outlier rejection, we found only a moderate pixelto-pixel correlation (FUV: 𝜌 = 0.536; NUV: 𝜌 = 0.243), owing to the large per-pixel scatter from 𝐻2 fluorescence, line emission and photon-counting noise (Fig. 2). This motivates the rejection and binning steps. Second, the Least Squares method: after rejecting outliers, we performed a weighted least-squares fit to the surviving individual pixels (Fig. 3), obtaining zero-reddening intercepts (offsets) of 278.6 (FUV) and 547.2 (NUV) photons cm -2 s -1 sr -1 ˚A -1 . Third, the Binning after rejection (centroid) method: we grouped the surviving pixels into equal 0.003 mag bins of E(B-V) , took the mean GALEX intensity in each bin, and fitted these binned centroids. The parameters for all cases are listed in Table 1. The three methods yield mutually consistent results. turns.question: Going back to my first question: what exactly did the paper say about it, and on which page?

public_answer.answer:
In «Far-Ultraviolet diffuse emission as a tracer of Galactic extinction at the North Galactic Pole-with-annotations», the authors test whether diffuse ultraviolet light tracks dust reddening by comparing GALEX ultraviolet intensity maps with Planck’s E(B−V) reddening map around the North Galactic Pole, at Galactic latitudes above 70°. They explain that dust scatters starlight into the far-ultraviolet, so its diffuse intensity should rise with reddening. The study is limited to this high-latitude, low-reddening region. [1]

The evidence is not simply a strong raw pixel-by-pixel correlation: the paper reports a moderate FUV correlation of 0.536, attributing the scatter to other ultraviolet emission and photon-counting noise. After estimating uncertainties, rejecting outliers, and averaging pixels in reddening bins, the FUV correlation rises to 0.993. The resulting reported relation is FUV intensity = 2285.3 × E(B−V) + 278.6, in the paper’s stated photon-intensity units. The authors interpret this as showing that FUV glow tracks dust reddening once scatter is reduced. These results are described on pages 2–3. [2] [3] [4]

As an additional check, they compare the FUV map with neutral-hydrogen column density, an independent tracer of the material associated with dust. The binned comparison has a reported correlation of 0.991; the conclusion summarizes this as evidence that FUV diffuse emission traces the gas and dust column. This appears on pages 3–4 and is reiterated on page 8. [5] [6] [7]

I read the paper’s extracted text across all its pages. I did not interpret the figures or formulas visually, and reading this one paper is not a search of the repository.

saved_turn.answer:
In «Far-Ultraviolet diffuse emission as a tracer of Galactic extinction at the North Galactic Pole-with-annotations», the authors test whether diffuse ultraviolet light tracks dust reddening by comparing GALEX ultraviolet intensity maps with Planck’s E(B−V) reddening map around the North Galactic Pole, at Galactic latitudes above 70°. They explain that dust scatters starlight into the far-ultraviolet, so its diffuse intensity should rise with reddening. The study is limited to this high-latitude, low-reddening region. [1]

The evidence is not simply a strong raw pixel-by-pixel correlation: the paper reports a moderate FUV correlation of 0.536, attributing the scatter to other ultraviolet emission and photon-counting noise. After estimating uncertainties, rejecting outliers, and averaging pixels in reddening bins, the FUV correlation rises to 0.993. The resulting reported relation is FUV intensity = 2285.3 × E(B−V) + 278.6, in the paper’s stated photon-intensity units. The authors interpret this as showing that FUV glow tracks dust reddening once scatter is reduced. These results are described on pages 2–3. [2] [3] [4]

As an additional check, they compare the FUV map with neutral-hydrogen column density, an independent tracer of the material associated with dust. The binned comparison has a reported correlation of 0.991; the conclusion summarizes this as evidence that FUV diffuse emission traces the gas and dust column. This appears on pages 3–4 and is reiterated on page 8. [5] [6] [7]

I read the paper’s extracted text across all its pages. I did not interpret the figures or formulas visually, and reading this one paper is not a search of the repository.

reopened_transcript.question: how do they show that the ultraviolet glow of the sky tracks how much dust dims starlight?
reopened_transcript.answer:
They test this in the low-dust North Galactic Pole region, comparing GALEX maps of diffuse ultraviolet light with Planck’s \(E(B-V)\) reddening map—a measure of how much dust reddens and dims starlight. Both maps were put on the same 6-arcminute grid, and the analysis was restricted to Galactic latitudes \(b>70^\circ\). [1] [2]

The evidence is a positive, roughly linear relation between ultraviolet brightness and reddening. But it is noisy pixel by pixel: the raw FUV correlation was only \(\rho=0.536\), which the authors attribute to other UV emission and photon-counting noise. They estimated pixel uncertainties, rejected outliers, then averaged surviving pixels in narrow reddening bins. The binned FUV relation was much tighter, \(\rho=0.993\), with fitted relation \(\mathrm{FUV}=2285.3\,E(B-V)+278.6\). In other words, after accounting for scatter, brighter diffuse FUV generally marks more reddening. [3] [4]

They also check the inferred dust map against other measures: it correlates strongly with neutral hydrogen column density, and its quasar-based extinction estimates agree closely with Planck’s; comparison with a Pan-STARRS stellar reddening map also favors the GALEX-based values in this region. [5]

So the claim is supported by a map-to-map trend plus independent checks—not by UV brightness alone. The direct pixel-level relationship is considerably weaker than the binned one, and the study’s result is for the North Galactic Pole, not yet a demonstration that the same relation holds across the whole sky. [3] [6]

reopened_transcript.question: Going back to my first question: what exactly did the paper say about it, and on which page?
reopened_transcript.answer:
In «Far-Ultraviolet diffuse emission as a tracer of Galactic extinction at the North Galactic Pole-with-annotations», the authors test whether diffuse ultraviolet light tracks dust reddening by comparing GALEX ultraviolet intensity maps with Planck’s E(B−V) reddening map around the North Galactic Pole, at Galactic latitudes above 70°. They explain that dust scatters starlight into the far-ultraviolet, so its diffuse intensity should rise with reddening. The study is limited to this high-latitude, low-reddening region. [1]

The evidence is not simply a strong raw pixel-by-pixel correlation: the paper reports a moderate FUV correlation of 0.536, attributing the scatter to other ultraviolet emission and photon-counting noise. After estimating uncertainties, rejecting outliers, and averaging pixels in reddening bins, the FUV correlation rises to 0.993. The resulting reported relation is FUV intensity = 2285.3 × E(B−V) + 278.6, in the paper’s stated photon-intensity units. The authors interpret this as showing that FUV glow tracks dust reddening once scatter is reduced. These results are described on pages 2–3. [2] [3] [4]

As an additional check, they compare the FUV map with neutral-hydrogen column density, an independent tracer of the material associated with dust. The binned comparison has a reported correlation of 0.991; the conclusion summarizes this as evidence that FUV diffuse emission traces the gas and dust column. This appears on pages 3–4 and is reiterated on page 8. [5] [6] [7]

I read the paper’s extracted text across all its pages. I did not interpret the figures or formulas visually, and reading this one paper is not a search of the repository.

reopened_transcript.question: how do they show that the ultraviolet glow of the sky tracks how much dust dims starlight?
reopened_transcript.answer:
They test this in the low-dust North Galactic Pole region, comparing GALEX maps of diffuse ultraviolet light with Planck’s \(E(B-V)\) reddening map—a measure of how much dust reddens and dims starlight. Both maps were put on the same 6-arcminute grid, and the analysis was restricted to Galactic latitudes \(b>70^\circ\). [1] [2]

The evidence is a positive, roughly linear relation between ultraviolet brightness and reddening. But it is noisy pixel by pixel: the raw FUV correlation was only \(\rho=0.536\), which the authors attribute to other UV emission and photon-counting noise. They estimated pixel uncertainties, rejected outliers, then averaged surviving pixels in narrow reddening bins. The binned FUV relation was much tighter, \(\rho=0.993\), with fitted relation \(\mathrm{FUV}=2285.3\,E(B-V)+278.6\). In other words, after accounting for scatter, brighter diffuse FUV generally marks more reddening. [3] [4]

They also check the inferred dust map against other measures: it correlates strongly with neutral hydrogen column density, and its quasar-based extinction estimates agree closely with Planck’s; comparison with a Pan-STARRS stellar reddening map also favors the GALEX-based values in this region. [5]

So the claim is supported by a map-to-map trend plus independent checks—not by UV brightness alone. The direct pixel-level relationship is considerably weaker than the binned one, and the study’s result is for the North Galactic Pole, not yet a demonstration that the same relation holds across the whole sky. [3] [6]

7 CONCLUSION We have constructed a far-ultraviolet (FUV) extinction map of the North Galactic Pole region (𝑏 > 70 ◦ ), where the reddening is low (E(B-V) < 0.1 mag), and assessed dust-scattered FUV diffuse emission as a tracer of Galactic extinction. A direct pixel-to-pixel regression yielded only moderate correlations (𝜌 = 0.536 for FUV and 𝜌 = 0.243 for NUV). This scatter reflects the additional per-pixel contributions frommolecular-hydrogen fluorescence, interstellar line emission, and photon-counting noise rather than a weakness of the underlying relation. To recover the intrinsic relation, we constructed per-pixel GALEX uncertainty maps. We applied a centroid-fitting method to estimate the mean intensity in E(B-V) bins after iteratively sigma-clipping outliers. This increased the correlations to 𝜌 = 0.993 (FUV) and 𝜌 = 0.976 (NUV) and gave the best-fit relations FUV = 2285.3 E(B - V) +278.6 and NUV = 1517.6 E(B - V) +547.2 (photon units). The fitted offsets are consistent with the non-reddeningcorrelated background (extragalactic background light and airglow) reported in previous works (Akshaya et al. 2018, 2019). Inverting these relations, we produced a 601 × 601 GALEX-based reddening map of the NGP. We validated the maps in three independent ways. First, both the GALEX and Planck maps correlate strongly with the H I column density from the HI4PI survey (HI4PI Collaboration et al. 2016) (𝜌 = 0.991 and 0.988, respectively), confirming that the FUV diffuse emission traces the gas and dust column. Second, using SDSS quasars as extragalactic extinction calibrators, the quasar extinctions derived from the GALEX and Planck maps agree closely (correlation 0.99, slope 0.986). Third, a comparison with the Pan-STARRS1 stellar reddening map of Schlafly et al. (2014) shows that the GALEX-based reddening has a smaller mean difference (0.039 mag, 𝜎 = 0.019) than the Planck-based reddening (0.064 mag, 𝜎 = 0.034), indicating that the FUV-derived map is at least as accurate as the thermal-dust map at high Galactic latitude. Figure 12. QSO extinction measured using GALEX in comparison with stellar observations of Pan-STARRS1 by Schlafly et al. (2014)(right). Side by side is plotted with Planck (left) and Schlafly et al. The mean fit of the extinction values of the quasars is shown by the blue line.

7.1 Future work A potential advantage of far-ultraviolet diffuse emission as an extinction tracer is its finer native pixel scale compared to Planck's data. Planck achieves a maximum resolution of approximately 6 ′ , whereas GALEX (Morrissey et al. 2007; Murthy 2025) provides farultraviolet diffuse emission maps at a resolution of 15 ′′ . As part of future efforts, we plan to extend the analysis to regions below 𝑏 = 70 ◦ , testing whether the FUV-Planck relation derived here for the North Galactic Pole holds at other, lower Galactic latitudes. This would allow dereddening corrections to be validated over a larger sky area, and facilitate analysis of dust properties using an independent tracer relative to Planck. The GALEX and Planck reddening maps of the North Galactic Pole produced in this work are publicly available at https://github.com/swagatastro98/NGP_resources.

reopened_transcript.question: Going back to my first question: what exactly did the paper say about it, and on which page?
reopened_transcript.answer:
In «Far-Ultraviolet diffuse emission as a tracer of Galactic extinction at the North Galactic Pole-with-annotations», the authors test whether diffuse ultraviolet light tracks dust reddening by comparing GALEX ultraviolet intensity maps with Planck’s E(B−V) reddening map around the North Galactic Pole, at Galactic latitudes above 70°. They explain that dust scatters starlight into the far-ultraviolet, so its diffuse intensity should rise with reddening. The study is limited to this high-latitude, low-reddening region. [1]

The evidence is not simply a strong raw pixel-by-pixel correlation: the paper reports a moderate FUV correlation of 0.536, attributing the scatter to other ultraviolet emission and photon-counting noise. After estimating uncertainties, rejecting outliers, and averaging pixels in reddening bins, the FUV correlation rises to 0.993. The resulting reported relation is FUV intensity = 2285.3 × E(B−V) + 278.6, in the paper’s stated photon-intensity units. The authors interpret this as showing that FUV glow tracks dust reddening once scatter is reduced. These results are described on pages 2–3. [2] [3] [4]

As an additional check, they compare the FUV map with neutral-hydrogen column density, an independent tracer of the material associated with dust. The binned comparison has a reported correlation of 0.991; the conclusion summarizes this as evidence that FUV diffuse emission traces the gas and dust column. This appears on pages 3–4 and is reiterated on page 8. [5] [6] [7]

I read the paper’s extracted text across all its pages. I did not interpret the figures or formulas visually, and reading this one paper is not a search of the repository.

citations.quote: 1 INTRODUCTION Interstellar extinction refers to the attenuation of starlight caused by absorption and scattering as it passes through the interstellar medium and must be corrected for in order to derive the intrinsic spectrum of any source in the sky. Accurate determination of extinction depends on the availability of nearby stars of known spectral type whose extinction can be measured as a function of wavelength (Fitzpatrick 1999; Fitzpatrick & Massa 2007) and large-scale surveys used proxies such as 21 cm radiation (Burstein & Heiles 1978) and, more recently, the infrared emission from thermally emitting dust grains (Schlegel et al. 1998). The current maps are those from Planck data (Planck Collaboration et al. 2014) at a spatial resolution of ∼ 5 ′ - 6 ′ . However, the infrared emission is dependent on the composition and size distribution of the grains and the temperature of each component and the conversion from observed surface brightness to reddening may be variable over the sky (Casandjian et al. 2022). Boissier et al. (2015) proposed that a better tracer of extinction at higher spatial resolution would be the far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX). The dust is optically thin at high Galactic latitudes, and dust-scattered far-UV (FUV) light should serve as a better tracer of extinction at higher spatial resolution than possible from available infrared observations. ★ E-mail: shalima.p@manipal.edu We have used GALEX observations to derive an extinction map around the North Galactic Pole (NGP), where the extinction is low (E(B-V) < 0.1 mag). The diffuse FUV here is dominated by dustscattered starlight (the diffuse Galactic light), which is directly proportional to the reddening. Other Galactic emission from the interstellar medium-molecular-hydrogen fluorescence, two-photon continuum, and line emission, also scales with the gas column, while a large constant offset arises from the extragalactic background light and airglow (Akshaya et al. 2019; Murthy 2014). We describe the data collection and processing in Section 2 and present the data analysis in Section 3. In Section 3 we also derive the extinction of quasars from our GALEX FUV and Planck maps and examine their relation with redshift (z), and we test the reddening derived from the GALEX FUV in the following sections. We compare our results with the optical stellar observations of Schlafly et al. (2014) and the quasar extinction maps with both the GALEX and Planck maps, and finally conclude on the use of FUV emission as a tracer of extinction relative to Planck or Schlegel.

3 DATAANALYSIS The Far-ultraviolet and Near-ultraviolet GALEX surface brightness is correlated with the reddening from Planck Collaboration et al. (2016b). We first found the correlation using all the pixels of GALEX FUV and NUV map with respect to Planck Collaboration et al. (2016a). In the first step, we only used the latitude cut; 𝑏 > 70 ◦ , as shown in Fig. 2. We found a moderate correlation between FUV and Planck (𝜌 = 0.536), but a lower correlation between NUV and Planck (𝜌 = 0.243). The high pixel-to-pixel scatter between the GALEX and Planck maps has two distinct origins. The first is astrophysical: the GALEX bands contain additional diffuse emission that is absent from the Planck reddening map - molecular-hydrogen fluorescence, two-photon continuum, and interstellar line emission. FUV photons absorbed by molecular hydrogen (𝐻2) excite it to a higher electronic state, and the subsequent radiative de-excitation emits fluorescent photons in the FUV range (1450-1750 ˚A; Murthy 2014). The second origin is purely statistical: the low photon-count rates of the diffuse UV background produce Poisson noise in individual pixels Ananthamoorthy et al. (2024). The astrophysical terms add a genuine signal that does not correlate with the Planck reddening, whereas the statistical term is random per-pixel noise; both increase the scatter and motivate the uncertainty-weighted, binned analysis described below. 1 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13337911 We constructed per-pixel uncertainty maps for both GALEX bands from the spatial scatter of the diffuse flux. On a 6 ′ grid matching the intensity maps, each pixel contains several native 2 ′ bins from every GALEX visit that covers it. For each visit (a single GALEX pointing), we computed the variance of those bin fluxes within the pixel, and the pixel uncertainty is the square root of the mean of these per-visit variances over all visits in that pixel (Equation 1).

The uncertainty is given in the same photon units as the intensity maps, photons cm -2 s -1 sr -1 ˚A -1 .

Second, the Least Squares method: after rejecting outliers, we performed a weighted least-squares fit to the surviving individual pixels (Fig. 3), obtaining zero-reddening intercepts (offsets) of 278.6 (FUV) and 547.2 (NUV) photons cm -2 s -1 sr -1 ˚A -1 . Third, the Binning after rejection (centroid) method: we grouped the surviving pixels into equal 0.003 mag bins of E(B-V) , took the mean GALEX intensity in each bin, and fitted these binned centroids. The parameters for all cases are listed in Table 1. The three methods yield mutually consistent results. public_answer.answer:
They model the ionospheric Faraday rotation with Spinifex and apply scan-by-scan corrections using DP3. They also include the modeled ionospheric effect in the 3C286 calibrator model before solving for polarization calibration terms. [1] [2]

The correction is not exact: the authors estimate an uncertainty of about 0.4 rad/m² in the ionospheric RM calculation and report a small remaining polarization-angle offset from the calibrator model. [3]

citations.text: Appendix A.3: Target self-calibration and subtraction of M87 After deriving the solution tables from the calibrators, we apply them to each of the four target fields before they are averaged using linear interpolation in both time and frequency. In detail these solution tables are the delay, phase and residual amplitude solutions of the gain calibrator, the amplitude, bandpass and leakage solutions of the bandpass calibrator, and the crosshand delay and crosshand phase solutions of the polarisation calibrator. Afterwards we average the target fields and apply ionospheric Faraday rotation corrections using again Spinifex and DP3 for each individual scan of each target field. The contribution of the ionospheric RM is usually low for the frequency range of the L-band. We find this as well for the fields in our observations. The mean ionospheric RM across the fields is -0.8 rad/m 2 . The ionospheric RM values for each field separately are reported in Table A.1. The self-calibration of the target fields is done using the selfcalibration software facetselfcal. This software iteratively images the field to create a model column, derives antenna-based calibration solutions and applies them to the data, using DP3 and in our case WSClean as an imager. We use facetselfcal for direction-independent calibration only, as no bright source is causing artefacts within the fields. In total, we run four rounds of calibration, starting with two rounds of scalar phase calibration followed by another two rounds of scalar complex gain calibration on the total intensity emission. The phase-only calibration we set the -multiscale parameter and image the data at a pixelscale of 2" for an image with a size of 6000 pixels to deconvolve any potential bright sources that could affect the field. Fig. A.4: Leakage calibration solutions for a single observation. The left plot shows the amplitude solution, the right one the phase solution. Fig. A.6: Phase frequency plot of the crosshand visibilities of the polarisation calibrator after application of all calibration solutions. After self-calibration we remove the effects caused by M87. By imaging the target fields phase shifted to M87, we are able to measure the flux of the contamination of M87 into each target field. If this flux is higher than 5σ of the surrounding noise, we use the MODEL_DATA column produced during the imaging and subtract it from the data. This way we remove the residual effects of M87 on the target fields whenever necessary. For the fields regarded in this study, we used the simplest subtraction method of M87 where we do not subtract the field prior to phase shifting and imaging of M87. This is applicable for these fields as they are not strongly affected by M87. For fields closer to M87, however, the subtraction of the field before phase shift- Fig. A.5: Crosshand phase solution for a single observation.

For the polarisation calibration we have set a frequency dependent full polarisation model. Hugo & Perley (2024) have derived a new model for the polarisation angle and polarised intensity of the polarisation calibrator 3C286 at frequencies below 12GHz, which we implement for the frequency range of the Lband. Computing the ionosphere with spinifex, we can corrupt the model for the effects of the ionosphere using DP3. The subsequent polarisation solutions are then derived against a model that already includes the expected ionospheric Faraday rotation. Following again the two step approach as before, we calibrate again for the delay and phase with solint = 'inf', deriving a single solution in time. We then apply the solution together with the previous ones to the polarisation calibrator before flagging the visibilities and recalculating the phase for a shorter solution interval of 30 seconds. In this step we also determine the normalised scalar amplitude solutions for the polarisation calibrator. After applying all solutions again we solve for the crosshand delay (Kcross) and for the crosshand phase (Xf), accounting for any ionospheric changes. Kcross we solve for using a solution interval of 30 seconds to account for temporal variations. For the crosshand phase specifically we ensure a robust solution by solving in 20MHz bins instead of for each channel, and by correcting for phase ambiguities in the solutions. This is done by determining the mean phase of the solution and checking if any step across frequency shows a shift of more than 90 degrees. If that is the case a phase of 180 degrees is added to this step. Such shifts are usually caused by the ambiguity of the direction of the polarisation vector (no visible difference can be seen between a polarisation vector at 0 degrees and one rotated by 180 degrees). Therefore adding these 180 degrees potentially fixes the solution steps in frequency that are not in line with the surrounding solution phases. As these solutions are not modified during self-calibration of the target field, it is important to ensure that crosshand phase solutions behave as expected and that the applied solutions to the polarisation calibrator show no strong deviations. Fig. A.5 and Fig. A.6 show the crosshand solutions and the visibilities in the crosshands for the polarisation calibrator for one of our observations. For the crosshand phase small variations between 10 and 20 degrees are a good indication that the solutions are not affected by RFI. For the visibilities, the phase against frequency plot reveals any remaining RFI or even bad calibration through deviations from mean value of zero. For the crosshand phase in our calibration we can see that the variations are less than 20 degrees. However, in the crosshands of the polarisation calibrator remaining RFI can still be seen, indicating that the flagging strategy and derivation of the calibration solutions has still room for improvement.

4. Discussion 4.1. ViMS pipeline performance and polarised source density In Sec. 2 we introduced the ViMS pipeline used for calibration, imaging and RM synthesis of the data, focusing on the polarisation calibration. Producing reliable polarisation information is therefore of main interest. As shown by the calibration diagnostics in Appendix A, the solutions are generally well behaved. When applied to the polarisation calibrator, the behaviour is as expected although some regions with leftover RFI are still visible, which indicates that the flagging strategy can still be improved. The derived Q, U and V values from the calibrator source are all within 3σ of the input model values. The measured polarisation fraction of the polarisation calibrator agrees well within 1σ with the model by Hugo & Perley (2024) and does not vary by more than 0.1%. The polarisation angle deviates by about 3.3σ from the model value, but only within a fraction of a degree in between each other. The offset in polarisation angle in regards to the model might be connected to the uncertainty in the ionospheric RM calculation of ∼ 0.4 rad/m 2 which corresponds to 2 degrees at 1.4 GHz. In that case, we would expect a distribution around the model value, but our polarisation angles are consistently smaller than the model's and only vary by 0.3 degree between the three different observations. This could be a coincidence given that only three observations are regarded. However, Loi et al. (2025) report an offset of approximately seven degrees in the polarisation angle, regardless of the used calibration tool (CASA, CASA Team et al. 2022; CARACal, Józsa et al. 2020) which is not mitigated when the ionospheric RM is taken into account. We could be seeing a reduced version of this effect in our data. Relative to other MeerKAT calibration workflows, the ViMS pipeline follows similar cross-calibration steps. Its strength lies more in the treatment of the polarisation calibration, with multiple flagging steps specifically for the crosshand visibilities and its inclusion of ionospheric contributions. With the subtraction of M87, it also takes the local conditions of the Virgo cluster into account, during the calibration of each field. We have seen that this reduces the noise in total emission by ∼ 2µJy/beam and therefore effectively increases the sensitivity in the field. The pipeline, however, follows a single strategy for calibration and requires a careful RFI mitigation before and during calibration and therefore manual inspection unlike a more automated calibration. It is also debatable whether some steps implemented in the pipeline improve the calibration, namely the setting of an accurate model for the polarisation calibrator. In our setup we corrupt the polarisation calibrator model with the ionosphere to solve the crosshand phase and delay against it. Comparing this to a calibration run without corrupting for the ionosphere reveals that the changes in the derived RM of the calibrator are negligibly small (the difference is approximately 0.1 rad/m 2 ).

citations.quote: Appendix A.3: Target self-calibration and subtraction of M87 After deriving the solution tables from the calibrators, we apply them to each of the four target fields before they are averaged using linear interpolation in both time and frequency. In detail these solution tables are the delay, phase and residual amplitude solutions of the gain calibrator, the amplitude, bandpass and leakage solutions of the bandpass calibrator, and the crosshand delay and crosshand phase solutions of the polarisation calibrator. Afterwards we average the target fields and apply ionospheric Faraday rotation corrections using again Spinifex and DP3 for each individual scan of each target field. The contribution of the ionospheric RM is usually low for the frequency range of the L-band. We find this as well for the fields in our observations. The mean ionospheric RM across the fields is -0.8 rad/m 2 . The ionospheric RM values for each field separately are reported in Table A.1. The self-calibration of the target fields is done using the selfcalibration software facetselfcal. This software iteratively images the field to create a model column, derives antenna-based calibration solutions and applies them to the data, using DP3 and in our case WSClean as an imager. We use facetselfcal for direction-independent calibration only, as no bright source is causing artefacts within the fields. In total, we run four rounds of calibration, starting with two rounds of scalar phase calibration followed by another two rounds of scalar complex gain calibration on the total intensity emission. The phase-only calibration we set the -multiscale parameter and image the data at a pixelscale of 2" for an image with a size of 6000 pixels to deconvolve any potential bright sources that could affect the field. Fig. A.4: Leakage calibration solutions for a single observation. The left plot shows the amplitude solution, the right one the phase solution. Fig. A.6: Phase frequency plot of the crosshand visibilities of the polarisation calibrator after application of all calibration solutions. After self-calibration we remove the effects caused by M87. By imaging the target fields phase shifted to M87, we are able to measure the flux of the contamination of M87 into each target field. If this flux is higher than 5σ of the surrounding noise, we use the MODEL_DATA column produced during the imaging and subtract it from the data. This way we remove the residual effects of M87 on the target fields whenever necessary. For the fields regarded in this study, we used the simplest subtraction method of M87 where we do not subtract the field prior to phase shifting and imaging of M87. This is applicable for these fields as they are not strongly affected by M87. For fields closer to M87, however, the subtraction of the field before phase shift- Fig. A.5: Crosshand phase solution for a single observation.

Hugo & Perley (2024) have derived a new model for the polarisation angle and polarised intensity of the polarisation calibrator 3C286 at frequencies below 12GHz, which we implement for the frequency range of the Lband. Computing the ionosphere with spinifex, we can corrupt the model for the effects of the ionosphere using DP3. The subsequent polarisation solutions are then derived against a model that already includes the expected ionospheric Faraday rotation. Following again the two step approach as before, we calibrate again for the delay and phase with solint = 'inf', deriving a single solution in time. We then apply the solution together with the previous ones to the polarisation calibrator before flagging the visibilities and recalculating the phase for a shorter solution interval of 30 seconds. In this step we also determine the normalised scalar amplitude solutions for the polarisation calibrator. After applying all solutions again we solve for the crosshand delay (Kcross) and for the crosshand phase (Xf), accounting for any ionospheric changes. Kcross we solve for using a solution interval of 30 seconds to account for temporal variations. For the crosshand phase specifically we ensure a robust solution by solving in 20MHz bins instead of for each channel, and by correcting for phase ambiguities in the solutions. This is done by determining the mean phase of the solution and checking if any step across frequency shows a shift of more than 90 degrees. If that is the case a phase of 180 degrees is added to this step. Therefore adding these 180 degrees potentially fixes the solution steps in frequency that are not in line with the surrounding solution phases. As these solutions are not modified during self-calibration of the target field, it is important to ensure that crosshand phase solutions behave as expected and that the applied solutions to the polarisation calibrator show no strong deviations. However, in the crosshands of the polarisation calibrator remaining RFI can still be seen, indicating that the flagging strategy and derivation of the calibration solutions has still room for improvement.

Producing reliable polarisation information is therefore of main interest. As shown by the calibration diagnostics in Appendix A, the solutions are generally well behaved. When applied to the polarisation calibrator, the behaviour is as expected although some regions with leftover RFI are still visible, which indicates that the flagging strategy can still be improved. The derived Q, U and V values from the calibrator source are all within 3σ of the input model values. The measured polarisation fraction of the polarisation calibrator agrees well within 1σ with the model by Hugo & Perley (2024) and does not vary by more than 0.1%. The polarisation angle deviates by about 3.3σ from the model value, but only within a fraction of a degree in between each other. The offset in polarisation angle in regards to the model might be connected to the uncertainty in the ionospheric RM calculation of ∼ 0.4 rad/m 2 which corresponds to 2 degrees at 1.4 GHz. In that case, we would expect a distribution around the model value, but our polarisation angles are consistently smaller than the model's and only vary by 0.3 degree between the three different observations. This could be a coincidence given that only three observations are regarded. However, Loi et al. (2025) report an offset of approximately seven degrees in the polarisation angle, regardless of the used calibration tool (CASA, CASA Team et al. 2022; CARACal, Józsa et al. 2020) which is not mitigated when the ionospheric RM is taken into account. We could be seeing a reduced version of this effect in our data. Relative to other MeerKAT calibration workflows, the ViMS pipeline follows similar cross-calibration steps. Its strength lies more in the treatment of the polarisation calibration, with multiple flagging steps specifically for the crosshand visibilities and its inclusion of ionospheric contributions. In our setup we corrupt the polarisation calibrator model with the ionosphere to solve the crosshand phase and delay against it. The offset in polarisation angle in regards to the model might be connected to the uncertainty in the ionospheric RM calculation of ∼ 0.4 rad/m 2 which corresponds to 2 degrees at 1.4 GHz. In that case, we would expect a distribution around the model value, but our polarisation angles are consistently smaller than the model's and only vary by 0.3 degree between the three different observations. This could be a coincidence given that only three observations are regarded. However, Loi et al. turns.question: with the next view not yet visible, how does the agent decide where to look?

public_answer.answer:
In «Towards Active Cross-View Object Geo-Localization», the agent **doesn’t preview the unseen images**. At each step, its policy uses the current localization state and which viewpoints it has already visited, then the view head scores the remaining viewpoint IDs and selects one. The paper describes 54 predefined viewpoints; previously visited ones are masked out. [1] [2]

It learns that choice from training: an offline oracle can evaluate candidate views and label the one that gives the greatest localization improvement, and supervised training teaches the policy to imitate those choices. Further policy refinement balances localization gains against the cost of acquiring more views. [3] [4] Thus, at runtime it chooses based on what it knows so far—not on seeing what the next view contains.

citations.text:
3 PROBLEM FORMULATION From passive CVOGL to ActiveGeo. Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) assumes a fixed query observation. In the UAV-based setting considered in this work, given a satellite reference image I s , a query UAV image Iv1 , and a prompt p specifying the target object, the model directly predicts its location ˆb as 

$$
\hat { b } = f ( I ^ { s } , I _ { v _ { 1 } } , p ) ,
$$

 where ˆb denotes the predicted target box. Since existing CVOGL relies entirely on the fixed query view Iv1 , it cannot acquire additional observations to resolve ambiguities and improve localization when the initial observation is unfavorable. In contrast, ActiveGeo allows a UAV agent to sequentially acquire observations from new viewpoints. Let V = {v1, . . . , vM} denote the candidate viewpoints. Each episode starts from an initial view Iv1 and a target prompt p. The prompt is provided only with the initial observation, while subsequent views must be associated with the same target without repeated prompting. At step t, let ˜ vt denote the viewpoint acquired, with ˜ v1 = v1. The observation history Ht is 

$$
\mathcal { H } _ { t } = \{ ( I _ { \tilde { v } _ { 1 } } , p ) , I _ { \tilde { v } _ { 2 } } , \dots , I _ { \tilde { v } _ { t } } \} ,
$$

 from which the model predicts the current localization ˆbt at step t 

$$
\hat { b } _ { t } = f ( I ^ { s } , \mathcal { H } _ { t } ) .
$$

 The agent then decides its action dt about whether to stop or continue, where dt ∈ {STOP, CONTINUE}. If it continues, it selects an unseen viewpoint ˜ vt+1 ∈ V \ V obs t , where V obs t denotes the viewpoints already acquired. The UAV then moves to ˜ vt+1 and obtains the corresponding observation, which is appended to Ht. If it stops, the current prediction ˆbt is returned as the final localization result. Embedding of Observation History is a MLP embedding of a binary view-status vector, where 1/0 indicates whether each viewpoint has been observed or not. Figure 2: Overall architecture of ActiveMoPT, an agent system for ActiveGeo that performs localization, viewpoint selection, and stopping. ActiveMoPT is initialized fromMoPT (Zhang et al., 2026b). At t = 1, before acquiring additional UAV views, its localizer is identical to MoPT. (a) The multi-view localizer updates the query state with newly acquired UAV views and predicts the target location on the satellite image. During Multi-View Prompt-Preserving Adaptation (Sec. 4.1), the encoders and Attninit are frozen. (b) The action policy decides whether to stop or acquire a new UAV view. Candidate UAV images are unavailable before selection, and the View Head selects among unobserved viewpoint IDs. Please refer to zoomed-in view for better visualization.

A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS Multi-view prompt-preserving adaptation. ActiveMoPT initializes its localizer from MoPT (Zhang et al., 2026b), with DINOv2-Base and CLIP ViT-L/14 (?) as the visual and language encoders. Images are resized to 512×512, and the localizer uses 256-dimensional states and 100 object queries. We train this stage for 24 epochs with 2-4 UAV observations per trajectory and a learning rate of 5×10-5 . A randomly sampled non-empty subset of P, B, and L is fixed throughout each trajectory. For LPI, we set the localization success threshold to τ = 0.5. Trajectory-guided policy initialization. We freeze the adapted localizer and train the 770Kparameter policy for 24 SFT epochs with a learning rate of 10-4 . The view head scores 54 candidate viewpoints, while the stop head predicts whether another observation is needed. During oracle trajectory generation, the oracle outputs STOP when the localization IoU exceeds 0.70. Otherwise, it selects the unseen viewpoint with the largest localization gain while this gain exceeds 0.015, and stops when no remaining viewpoint satisfies this condition. Each oracle trajectory contains at most 7 observations. The SFT checkpoint with the best closed-loop performance on MoP-UAV (Zhang et al., 2026b) is used to initialize the following GRPO stage. Cost-aware policy refinement. Starting from the selected SFT policy, we keep the localizer frozen and optimize only the policy for 2 GRPO epochs. Each episode uses groups of 32 sampled trajectories. The policy learning rate is 10-5 , the clipping radius is ϵc = 0.2, and the KL coefficient is β = 0.02. We set λ = 0.01. Viewpoint representation. Following the viewpoint setting of University-1652 (Zheng et al., 2020), each satellite image is associated with 54 predefined UAV viewpoints. These viewpoints are sampled along three circular trajectories around the target from higher to lower elevations, resulting in 54 discrete viewpoint IDs. We therefore formulate viewpoint selection as a 54-way classification problem. Each ID corresponds to one fixed UAV viewpoint, and the view head predicts a score over the 54 IDs. At each step, viewpoints that have already been observed are masked out, and the highest-scoring remaining ID is selected when the policy decides to continue.

4.2 TRAJECTORY-GUIDED POLICY INITIALIZATION With the multi-view localizer in place, ActiveMoPT still needs to learn when to stop and which view to acquire next. Therefore, we introduce a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage (Fig. 3(a)) to initialize the action behavior, which provides a cold start and equips the model with a basic awareness of the action policy, ensuring the subsequent reinforcement learning (RL) explores within a meaningful policy space (Luo et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b). Construction of the oracle trajectory dataset. During training, all candidate UAV views and the ground-truth box are available for each scene. We use this information offline to construct supervised trajectories by evaluating candidate viewpoints and assigning an action at each step. Given the current observation history Ht, the frozen localizer produces a prediction ˆbt. Its IoU ut with the ground-truth box b∗ is 

$$
u _ { t } = I o U ( \hat { b } _ { t } , b ^ { * } ) .
$$

 For each unseen viewpoint v, we evaluate the frozen localizer using Ht together with Iv, and denote the resulting IoU by u(v) t+1 . The localization gain ∆u(v) t of this candidate is 

$$
\Delta u _ { t } ^ { ( v ) } = u _ { t + 1 } ^ { ( v ) } - u _ { t } .
$$

saved_turn.question: with the next view not yet visible, how does the agent decide where to look?
saved_turn.answer:
In «Towards Active Cross-View Object Geo-Localization», the agent **doesn’t preview the unseen images**. At each step, its policy uses the current localization state and which viewpoints it has already visited, then the view head scores the remaining viewpoint IDs and selects one. The paper describes 54 predefined viewpoints; previously visited ones are masked out. [1] [2]

It learns that choice from training: an offline oracle can evaluate candidate views and label the one that gives the greatest localization improvement, and supervised training teaches the policy to imitate those choices. Further policy refinement balances localization gains against the cost of acquiring more views. [3] [4] Thus, at runtime it chooses based on what it knows so far—not on seeing what the next view contains.

public_answer.answer:
In «Towards Active Cross-View Object Geo-Localization», the agent does **not** inspect candidate images before choosing. On **page 3**, the paper says the candidate UAV images are unavailable before selection and the View Head chooses among unobserved viewpoint IDs. [1]

For training, the paper describes constructing oracle trajectories by evaluating candidate views against the current observation history and labeling a view with the greatest localization gain when it exceeds a threshold; otherwise, the label is STOP (**page 5**). reopened_transcript.question: with the next view not yet visible, how does the agent decide where to look?
reopened_transcript.answer:
In «Towards Active Cross-View Object Geo-Localization», the agent **doesn’t preview the unseen images**. At each step, its policy uses the current localization state and which viewpoints it has already visited, then the view head scores the remaining viewpoint IDs and selects one. The paper describes 54 predefined viewpoints; previously visited ones are masked out. [1] [2]

It learns that choice from training: an offline oracle can evaluate candidate views and label the one that gives the greatest localization improvement, and supervised training teaches the policy to imitate those choices. Further policy refinement balances localization gains against the cost of acquiring more views. [3] [4] Thus, at runtime it chooses based on what it knows so far—not on seeing what the next view contains.

reopened_transcript.question: with the next view not yet visible, how does the agent decide where to look?
reopened_transcript.answer:
In «Towards Active Cross-View Object Geo-Localization», the agent **doesn’t preview the unseen images**. At each step, its policy uses the current localization state and which viewpoints it has already visited, then the view head scores the remaining viewpoint IDs and selects one. The paper describes 54 predefined viewpoints; previously visited ones are masked out. [1] [2]

It learns that choice from training: an offline oracle can evaluate candidate views and label the one that gives the greatest localization improvement, and supervised training teaches the policy to imitate those choices. Further policy refinement balances localization gains against the cost of acquiring more views. [3] [4] Thus, at runtime it chooses based on what it knows so far—not on seeing what the next view contains.

turns.question: what does Philippine labor law say about overtime pay?

public_answer.answer:
As general background—not a finding from CIT-U’s repository—Philippine labor law generally requires covered employees to receive overtime pay for work **beyond eight hours in a day**:

- **Ordinary workday:** at least **125% of the employee’s regular hourly rate** for each overtime hour.
- **Rest day or special non-working day:** at least **130% of the hourly rate for the first eight hours**; overtime hours are generally paid at **169%** of the regular hourly rate.
- **Regular holiday:** generally **200% for the first eight hours**; overtime hours are generally paid at **260%** of the regular hourly rate. Higher rates may apply when a holiday also falls on a rest day.

Some workers—such as certain managerial employees and field personnel—may be excluded from the Labor Code’s overtime-pay rules. The exact rate can depend on the day worked and the employee’s coverage, so check the applicable DOLE rules or get advice for a specific situation.

turns.question: what does the training loop do with a problem the model has not managed to solve yet?

public_answer.answer: If all the sampled completions for a problem are incorrect, the loop samples another batch for that same problem instead of immediately moving on. It repeats this until it finds a correct completion, but each time it continues only with probability \(p_{\text{NGU}}\); otherwise it gives up on that problem and moves to another. [1]

citations.text: 4 Countering the Matthew Effect with Never Give Up Not Resampling Easy Prompts The simplest solution has been to exclude problems that are too easy from being resampled later in training (An et al., 2025). The issue is that this changes our training distribution to be harder and harder assuming that our model will never regress on previously-solved problems. In Appendix C.2 we find that our baseline training runs can perfectly solve a problem, but regress on it later in training when implementing this filtering strategy. So this approach can improve on the hardest problems at the expense of performance on easier problems. Never Give Up Our goal is therefore to keep sampling from our full training distribution but more quickly filter easy prompts while reallocating compute to hard prompts. We propose never give up, a simple but effective way to leverage our asynchronous RL pipeline and reallocate compute to harder prompts. We first sample some small number of completions-per-prompt e.g. K = 4. If all our completions are correct, we can quickly filter this problem as too easy. If all our completions are wrong, the standard approach is to give up and sample another problem. Instead, we never give up (NGU) on solving this problem and sample K more completions, continuing until we solve the prompt. As certain problems may be too difficult, we actually continue sampling with probability pNGU and give up on the problem with probability 1 - pNGU. This creates a geometric distribution of the total number of samples, allowing us to occasionally sample many completions on difficult prompts but keeping the average number of samples at K 1-p . See pseudocode for NGU in Appendix E. We re-run our previous N = 64, K = 4 baseline but continue sampling with pNGU = 0.95. As shown in Figure 4, NGU outperforms all previous baselines with its pass@1 gains coming specifically on the extra hard problem subset. Looking at what prompts NGU trains on in Figure 5, we see that NGU gets the best of both large K and small K. Early in training, NGU has as many hard prompts in the batch as K = 32 but later in training it has as many as K = 4, achieving close to the pareto-optimal amount of hard prompts in the training batch. Similarly, NGU achieves the best of both K = 4 and K = 32 for filtering easy prompts. Key to NGU's success is an asynchronous RL infrastructure, so that quickly filtered easy prompts are replenished by harder prompts, therefore reallocating compute from easy to harder problems. We demonstrate the necessity of async RL for NGU and provide a detailed comparison to previous sync RL work (Xiong et al., 2025) in Appendix C.1

turns.question: how does the smaller model learn where each word sits in the audio?

public_answer.answer:
In «Alignment-Path Distillation from Non-streaming ASR-LLMs for Streaming Speech Recognition», a fixed, non-streaming teacher estimates which audio positions correspond to each transcript token using its text-to-audio attention. If an estimate is low-confidence, the method substitutes a forced-alignment estimate. [1]

The method then selects a monotonic sequence of audio positions, converts them to timestamps, and uses those timestamps to assign transcript tokens to audio chunks. [1] The smaller streaming model trains on these chunk-and-text sequences, learning to predict each token from the audio available so far. [2] The paper also describes optional distillation from the teacher’s output probabilities and internal representations. [3]

So the teacher’s alignment guides which chunk a token is trained with; the student learns to recognize and produce the transcript under that chunk-by-chunk setup.

citations.text:
2.2.1. Alignment-path distillation Attention extraction. We extract each text token's attention scores over audio embeddings from the non-streaming ASRLLM teacher, using its final LLM layer and averaging across all attention heads. Applying softmax over the audio positions yields an alignment matrix A ∈ RU×F , where U and F are the numbers of text and audio tokens, respectively. The text tokens correspond to the modeling units of the LLM. Each row Ai,: gives the attention distribution of text token i over audio tokens. Confidence-based FA fallback. Let AFA i,: denote the FA alignment distribution over audio tokens for text token i. When the peak attention probability si = maxj Aij over audio positions falls below θFA, we replace its attention distribution with the FA distribution: 

$$
\widetilde { A } _ { i , \colon } = \begin{cases} A _ { i , \colon } ^ { F A } , & s _ { i } < \theta _ { F A } , \\ A _ { i , \colon } , & \text {otherwise} . \end{cases} ( 2 )
$$

 Global monotonic anchor search. Independent peak selection can produce non-monotonic anchors. Applying a cumulative maximum afterwards may propagate an early mistake to subsequent units. Let ei denote the audio position index assigned to text unit i, and let e = (e0, . . . , eU-1) denote the alignment path. Inspired by monotonic alignment search in Glow-TTS [17], we optimize all anchors jointly using the updated alignment matrix ˜ A: 

$$
e ^ { * } = \arg \max _ { 0 \leq e _ { 0 } < \cdots < e _ { U \ 1 } < F } \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { U - 1 } \log ( \widetilde { A } _ { i , e _ { i } } + \epsilon ) , \quad ( 3 )
$$

2.1. Interleaved ASR-LLMArchitecture and Training The speech encoder extracts acoustic features, which the projector downsamples and maps to the LLM embedding space. The model processes consecutive audio chunks while retaining preceding audio and text as context. Following the interleaved training paradigm of UniASR [5], we divide speech into fixed-duration chunks and segment the reference transcript according to token alignment timestamps. Each audio chunk is followed by its assigned reference text. With audio embeddings ak and text embeddings y(k) , the LLM input is 

$$
[ a _ { 1 } , y ^ { ( 1 ) } , a _ { 2 } , y ^ { ( 2 ) } , \dots , a _ { K } , y ^ { ( K ) } ] , \quad ( 1 ) \quad p e a k
$$

 where K is the number of chunks. Text segments may be empty. The LLM predicts each text token conditioned on the available audio embeddings and preceding reference tokens. The cross-entropy loss LCE is computed over the target text tokens. Chunk-restricted encoder attention and causal LLM attention prevent access to subsequent audio chunks. During decoding, the embeddings of each incoming audio chunk are appended to the audio-text history of each beam hypothesis after encoding and projection. The LLM extends the hypotheses autoregressively using beam search, with a token limit per chunk. At each output update, we display the current highest-scoring hypothesis. Changes in the best hypothesis can revise previously displayed text, resulting in flicker. Audio processing and text generation alternate as new chunks arrive. where ϵ = 10-9 . The search selects one acoustic anchor per text unit and allows acoustic positions to be skipped. It differs from a duration path that assigns every acoustic frame to a text unit. Let V (i, j) be the largest sum of log-alignment probabilities for text units 0, . . . , i when unit i is assigned to audio position j. The recurrence is 

$$
V ( i , j ) = \log ( \tilde { A } _ { i , j } + \epsilon ) + \max _ { k < j } V ( i - 1 , k ) . \quad ( 4 ) \quad \text {proge} \quad \ e R e d
$$

 Prefix maxima and their indices allow this recurrence to be evaluated in O(UF) time. Backtracking from the best last-row position recovers the anchor sequence. Audio position indices are converted to timestamps using the time step of the projected features. These timestamps determine the text segments assigned to the fixed-duration audio chunks in the interleaved training sequence.

2.2. Alignment-path Distillation Framework The non-streaming model used to initialize the student is kept fixed as the teacher. The teacher-derived alignment path is used to construct the student's interleaved training sequence, with logit and hidden-state losses providing additional supervision.

reopened_transcript.question: how does the smaller model learn where each word sits in the audio?
reopened_transcript.answer:
In «Alignment-Path Distillation from Non-streaming ASR-LLMs for Streaming Speech Recognition», a fixed, non-streaming teacher estimates which audio positions correspond to each transcript token using its text-to-audio attention. If an estimate is low-confidence, the method substitutes a forced-alignment estimate. [1]

The method then selects a monotonic sequence of audio positions, converts them to timestamps, and uses those timestamps to assign transcript tokens to audio chunks. [1] The smaller streaming model trains on these chunk-and-text sequences, learning to predict each token from the audio available so far. [2] The paper also describes optional distillation from the teacher’s output probabilities and internal representations. [3]

So the teacher’s alignment guides which chunk a token is trained with; the student learns to recognize and produce the transcript under that chunk-by-chunk setup.
